Introduction - March 2011 











##### **Introduction** 

The base metals complex posted further gains in February. The GFMS Base Metal Index peaked at 393.67 on February 15, which represents an 8.3% improvement on the start of the year.  Near “perfect storm” conditions prevailed in February, which then encouraged some profit-taking. There has been a further bout of dollar weakness that has supported the price.  As discussed on pages E1-E2, the vast majority of the economic indicators remain broadly supportive for the base metals com

plex.  Although there are plenty of risks to this scenario – oil prices, general inflationary pressures, fiscal tightening in some markets, China, sovereign debt problems – our favoured economic indicators, the forward-looking purchasing managers indices and the OECD composite leading indicator, are all firmly in positive territory. 

###### **The mature economies - for every action a reaction?** 

A constant theme of our analysis was the exceptionally strong rebound in consumption within this region in 2010. In some cases, consumption more than made up for the 2009 losses and demand exceeded 2008 levels.  The fear was some inventory build had taken place and that there would be a reaction to last year’s performance.  Although a lot of the detailed information pertaining to non-ferrous metals demand is “lagging” rather than “leading”, most figures suggest that demand finished 2010 on a strong note and that this strength has been carried over to the first quarter of this year. 

We believe that the crude steel production data provides a reasonable (and timely) proxy for base metals demand, as the metals share a large number of end-use markets. The latest figures from the World Steel Association show a 5.3% year-on-year advance in production in January.  This came about despite an increase of just 0.5% in China and an estimated 0.5% decline in India.  Last year, global crude steel output increased by 15.2% to 1.495 billion tonnes. 

The myriad end-uses for stainless steel make it a good barometer of underlying demand conditions for the industrial metals, as well as driving the demand for nickel.  The International Stainless Steel Federation has just released its data for the fourth quarter.  Total stainless steel output increased by 14.1% year-on-year, while output was 3.4% higher than in the previous three months. 

###### **Producers and fabricators are upbeat** 

A number of key players have just released their results for 2010.  Generally they confirm the strong conditions that prevailed in 2010, which was characterised by both higher prices and higher shipments.  In particular, the nonferrous fabricators are pointing to healthy order books and generally lengthening lead times.  This tends to confirm the findings of our latest programme of field research carried out for the Copper Survey 2011.  Conditions in the North America market are particularly firm, which is in line with the generally upbeat economic numbers emanating from the region.  We do note that underlying activity in the European and, especially, the Japanese market, is not quite so robust. This is reflected in movements in physical premiums.  For example, second quarter aluminium premiums in Japan have been settled unchanged from first quarter levels, while copper premiums in Europe have hit a 15-month low. 

###### **China: more of the same?** 

It is always difficult to assess conditions in China during the first quarter.  The timing of the holiday shutdown inevitably affects ye

ar-on-year comparisons, while some data is not published for this period. Nevertheless, most of the data that is available for key end using markets, such as autos, suggest that the buoyant conditions seen in 2010 will be repeated in 2011. In terms of Chinese base metal demand, the sector should benefit from the relatively low level of pipeline inventories. The performance of the Eurozone economic sentiment index is somewhat at odds with the wider pessimism concerning the economic prospects for the region.  It registered 107.8, up from 106.8 in January.  The improvement is being driven by the mainstream economies notably Germany. The region at the moment appears to be able to shrug off issues such the strong euro, weak labour markets and fiscal tightening in some key countries. 

Japan’s industrial production rose solidly in January, driven by a better performance in the transport equipment, general machinery, and iron and steel industries. Recent signs of a strengthening global recovery bode well for Japan’s industrial sector, as many local producers are sensitive to external demand. Nevertheless, weak domestic demand will continue to put a cap on the level of the industrial recovery. 

It should be remembered that The Bank of Japan’s fourth quarter Tankan surve

y showed a broad-based deterioration in business sentiment. The fear is that the stronger currency could derail the recovery in the sector that has largely supported industrial production growth in 2010 and in early 2011. Both Chinese industrial production and fixed asset investment finished 2010 on a strong note rising by 13.5% and 24.5% respectively in December. In the absence of data for January and February due to the Chinese New Year, we assess the latest trade figures. The country’s trade surplus declined in January because of a rise in imports and a decline in exports compared with December. Higher commodity prices in general are pushing up China’s imports bill and expectations of higher prices may have prompted big firms to stock up on raw materials. As a result of this surge in output, and combined with the inventory build seen over 2009, the Chinese market is well supplied.
